title: Air India, Akasa Hike Fuel Surcharges Just as Diwali Travel Peaks
excerpt: Domestic surcharges now reach ₹1,200 per leg and North America–India flights carry $215 each way, as all four major carriers raise charges within four days on soaring jet fuel prices.
body:
• Air India, Air India Express and Akasa Air raised fuel surcharges on all new bookings from October 9, days after IndiGo's increase on October 6 — so every major Indian carrier has now moved within four days, right as Diwali travel demand peaks.
  • Air India's domestic surcharge now runs ₹400–₹1,200 per one-way sector by distance; international surcharges reach $215 to North America and $135 to Europe. Akasa charges ₹375–₹1,150 domestic and a flat ₹2,500 on select Gulf and Southeast Asia routes.
  • The driver: jet fuel prices rose about 13% on October 1 — the third straight monthly increase — with Delhi ATF around ₹137 a litre, crude above $100 a barrel on West Asia conflict, and the rupee near 97 to the dollar.
  • What this means for your Diwali flight: a Delhi–Mumbai return on Air India now carries roughly ₹800–₹1,200 extra in fuel charges alone; a Delhi–London return adds about $270 (₹26,000+) in surcharges before any base-fare movement.

Every airline moves within four days

Air travel is about to get more expensive for Diwali flyers. Air India, Air India Express and Akasa Air announced revised fuel surcharges on domestic and international flights on Thursday, effective on new bookings from October 9. The move follows IndiGo's increase, which took effect on October 6 — meaning all four major carriers raised charges within the same week, just as the festival travel rush begins.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=FVHbNOI80hg

Air India and its low-cost arm said the revision was intended to partially offset additional expenditure from higher aviation turbine fuel prices. "ATF prices have witnessed significant volatility in recent months, driven largely by geopolitical developments and sustained pressure on global energy markets," the airlines said in a statement. The new charges apply to Air India Express bookings made from midnight on October 9 and Air India bookings from 11 am the same day.

The new numbers

For Air India and Air India Express domestic one-way flights, the surcharge is ₹400 for sectors up to 500 km, ₹600 for 501–1,000 km, ₹850 for 1,001–1,500 km, and ₹1,200 for sectors of 1,501 km or more. That represents an increase of roughly 34 to 60 per cent over the previous distance-based structure introduced in April, under which domestic levies ranged from ₹299 to ₹899.

On international routes, Air India's revised surcharge is $215 for North America, $210 for Australia, $135 for Europe including the UK, and $55 for West Asia and the Middle East.

Akasa Air — which had withdrawn its domestic fuel surcharge earlier but is now reintroducing it — will levy ₹375 on domestic sectors up to 500 km, ₹600 on 501–1,000 km, ₹900 on 1,001–1,500 km and ₹1,150 on longer sectors. On select international routes — Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Thailand and Vietnam — a flat ₹2,500 surcharge applies. Akasa's changes take effect for all new bookings from 00:01 on October 9.

IndiGo's earlier revision, effective October 6, set its domestic charge at ₹375–₹1,300, with international charges going up to ₹10,000 on European routes.

Why now: fuel, war and the rupee

The trigger is simple arithmetic. State-run oil companies raised jet fuel prices by about 13 per cent on October 1 — the third consecutive monthly increase — taking Delhi ATF to roughly ₹137 a litre. Global crude is trading above $100 a barrel as the West Asia conflict disrupts supply, and the rupee's slide toward 97 to the dollar makes dollar-denominated fuel even costlier. Fuel can account for as much as 40 per cent of an Indian airline's operating costs.

Airlines also point to longer flight routings around restricted airspace in conflict zones, which burn more fuel per sector, and to India's high taxation on ATF, which keeps domestic fuel prices elevated regardless of global benchmarks.

The petroleum ministry has pushed back, saying there is no ATF supply crunch and no domestic price hike by oil companies — but airlines are passing through global market costs, not domestic supply shortages.

What it means for your Diwali trip

The surcharge is a fixed rupee or dollar amount baked into each ticket, and it is largest on long routes. A family of four flying Delhi–London on Air India this Diwali will pay roughly $540 — over ₹50,000 — in fuel surcharges alone on the return trip, before any movement in base fares or demand-driven pricing. Domestic flyers should add ₹800–₹2,400 to return fares on typical routes, on top of fares that are already elevated for the festival window.

The surcharge applies to new bookings, not tickets already issued — so travellers who booked before October 9 are unaffected. Both Air India and Akasa said they will review the charges periodically.

What's next

Watch crude prices and the rupee. If the West Asia conflict de-escalates and oil retreats below $100, airlines will face pressure to roll the surcharges back — IndiGo's shares fell 3.55% on October 8, a reminder that investors punish carriers for margin compression even when they can pass costs on. For now, the message for Diwali travellers is blunt: book early, compare across carriers, and budget for the surcharge line item.
